screens.title: Structural Patterns — Adapter and Decorator
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on two structural patterns that shape how objects relate and evolve in a system. First, Adapter solves the problem of incompatible interfaces: it translates one interface into another so existing classes can be used by new clients without changing either side. Think of a travel plug adapter that translates an unfamiliar plug shape so the device still gets power. Second, Decorator offers a way to add responsibilities to objects at runtime by wrapping them, avoiding subclass explosion when you need many feature combinations. You will encounter concrete Java examples: an OldLogger adapted to a NewLogger interface, and Coffee objects wrapped with Milk, Sugar, and Caramel decorators so costs and descriptions change dynamically. We will also compare object adapter versus class adapter, highlight common mistakes, and walk through hands-on starter tasks adapting a legacy payment gateway and decorating a basic editor. By the end of this chapter you’ll know when to translate an interface versus when to layer behavior, and you’ll be able to implement and combine these patterns in realistic Java code. Start by exploring the three topics shown below to build intuition before we dive into code and exercises.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Adapter & Decorator

Translate incompatible interfaces with Adapter, and compose behavior dynamically with Decorator to avoid subclass explosion.

In this lesson
Adapter: translate interfaces to use legacy or third-party code without changes.
Coming up
Decorator: wrap objects to add features like toppings on coffee at runtime.
Why it matters
Preserve existing code while adding flexibility and reducing brittle inheritance trees.
Visual concept
Adapter = Translator
Bridge between mismatched interfaces
Decorator = Wrapper
Add responsibilities without modifying the core object
Practical examples: adapting a legacy logger to a modern logging interface, and layering milk and sugar decorators on a coffee object to change description and cost.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you will use when designing maintainable systems. First, you will implement the Adapter pattern to convert an existing class interface into the interface your client expects. This includes writing an adapter that delegates calls to an adaptee instance. Second, you will distinguish class adapters (inheritance-based) from object adapters (composition-based), and understand why object adapters are usually preferred in Java. Third, you will identify scenarios where Adapter is the right choice, such as integrating legacy code or third-party libraries without modifying them. Each objective shows a clear skill and why it matters: adapters preserve working code and avoid risky rewrites. You will also implement the Decorator pattern to attach responsibilities to an object dynamically, and understand how this pattern offers a more flexible alternative to subclassing. Finally, you will apply decorators to real objects so behavior can be composed at runtime. Together these objectives prepare you to choose whether to translate an interface or to wrap behavior, and to implement both patterns safely in Java.

screens.title: What is the Adapter pattern?
screens.narratorSegment: Adapter is a structural pattern whose purpose is to make two incompatible interfaces work together. The pattern introduces an adapter class that implements the interface expected by the client and internally delegates calls to the adaptee, the existing class with a different A P I. A concrete example is adapting a legacy logger with a single logMessage method so it can be used where a client expects separate info and error methods. This avoids modifying stable legacy code or rewriting the client. Remember there are two implementation strategies: class adapter, which uses inheritance, and object adapter, which uses composition. In Java, object adapters are far more common because Java does not support multiple class inheritance; composition is safer and more flexible. A common misconception is to confuse Adapter with Facade. Adapter converts one interface to another for a specific client need, while Facade provides a simplified interface over a subsystem for many clients. When you need to adapt an old A P I to a new interface for a particular use, Adapter is the right fit. Consider whether you need to translate method signatures or to hide complexity; that distinction will guide your pattern choice.

keyIdea.title: Adapter defined
keyIdea.text: Adapter maps a target interface to an adaptee so incompatible classes can interoperate without change.

content.html:
Core Concept

Adapter — definition & analogy

Adapter converts an existing class's interface into the interface a client expects. Think of a travel plug adapter.

Definition
An adapter implements the target interface and delegates to an adaptee instance to translate calls.
When to use
Integrate legacy classes or third-party libraries whose APIs don't match your client code.
Misconception check
Adapter is not Facade: Adapter remaps an interface for compatibility; Facade simplifies a whole subsystem for clients.
Key Takeaway

Choose Adapter when you must reuse an existing class whose API cannot be changed but must match a client interface.

Analogy & example
Travel adapter analogy
A device plug (adaptee) has a different shape than the wall socket (target). The adapter translates the plug shape so the device gets power without changing the device or the socket.
Concrete example
An OldLogger with logMessage can be adapted to a NewLogger interface that expects info and error methods through an adapter that delegates and prefixes messages.

screens.title: Class Adapter vs Object Adapter
screens.narratorSegment: There are two conceptual implementation strategies for Adapter: class adapters and object adapters. Class adapters use inheritance: the adapter inherits from the adaptee and from the target interface type, effectively becoming both. This approach can work when adapting interfaces or in languages with multiple inheritance, but in Java it's rarely used because Java does not permit inheriting from two concrete classes. Object adapters use composition: the adapter implements the target interface and holds a reference to an adaptee instance. Calls on the adapter translate into calls on the adaptee. This composition approach is more flexible: you can adapt different concrete adaptees without changing the adapter class, and you avoid the brittle coupling inheritance creates. A simple process to implement an object adapter is: define the target interface, hold an adaptee instance inside the adapter, implement target methods by delegating or translating calls to the adaptee, and construct the adapter with a specific adaptee. A common mistake is attempting to force a class adapter design in Java; prefer composition and keep adapters small and focused on translating behavior, not re-implementing it.

keyIdea.title: Implementation advice
keyIdea.text: Prefer object adapters in Java: implement the target interface and delegate to an adaptee instance using composition.

content.html:
Process Flow

Class Adapter vs Object Adapter

1
Class Adapter
Adapter inherits and tries to be both target and adaptee. Not practical in Java for concrete classes.
2
Object Adapter
Adapter implements the target interface and holds an adaptee instance to which it delegates calls. Flexible and preferred in Java.
3
Implementation steps
Define target, accept an adaptee instance, implement methods by translating or delegating to adaptee, and construct the adapter with the adaptee.
Common mistake

Trying to use multiple inheritance or to re-implement adaptee logic in the adapter. Keep adapters thin and focused on translation.

Visual example
Object Adapter diagram (cards)
Target interface implemented by Adapter → Adapter contains Adaptee instance → Adapter delegates translated calls to Adaptee.
Why composition
Composition allows swapping adaptees at runtime and composes behavior without tight inheritance coupling.

screens.title: Object Adapter: OldLoggerAdapter example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete object adapter example that appears in the chapter source. We have an existing OldLogger class with a single method that logs messages in a legacy format. The new client expects a NewLogger interface with info and error methods. The adapter implements NewLogger and holds an OldLogger instance. When the client calls info on the adapter, the adapter translates that into a logMessage call on the OldLogger, typically adding a prefix like INFO. The same goes for error. This translation preserves the legacy implementation while matching the client's expectations. When reading the code, pay attention to delegation and to how the adapter's constructor receives the adaptee instance — that dependency injection keeps the adapter testable and decoupled from concrete adaptee construction. A misconception is to implement heavy logic inside the adapter; instead, keep translations small and clear. After you read the code panel, imagine substituting a different logging adaptee: the adapter remains the same because it depends on the adaptee interface or concrete instance handed to it. Object Adapter: OldLoggerAdapter example means keep adapter logic minimal: translate signatures and delegate behavior. inject the adaptee so the adapter remains testable.. In practical terms, walk through the adapter that makes oldlogger fulfill newlogger. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

OldLoggerAdapter (object adapter)

Study how the adapter implements the new interface and delegates to the old logger instance.
<!-- Java code shown for study; angle brackets escaped for safe HTML -->
// The Adaptee: The existing class with an incompatible interface
class OldLogger {
  public void logMessage(String message) {
    System.out.println("OLD LOGGER: " + message);
  }
}

// The Target: The interface your client expects
interface NewLogger {
  void info(String message);
  void error(String message);
}

// The Adapter: Converts OldLogger's interface to NewLogger's interface
class OldLoggerAdapter implements NewLogger {
  private OldLogger oldLogger;

  public OldLoggerAdapter(OldLogger oldLogger) {
    this.oldLogger = oldLogger;
  }

  @Override
  public void info(String message) {
    oldLogger.logMessage("INFO: " + message);
  }

  @Override
  public void error(String message) {
    oldLogger.logMessage("ERROR: " + message);
  }
}
Explanation & example
Delegation
The adapter translates each NewLogger method into a call to OldLogger.logMessage and adds a severity prefix.
Dependency injection
Passing an OldLogger instance into the adapter constructor keeps the adapter decoupled and testable.
Example run
Client code creates OldLogger and wraps it with OldLoggerAdapter so performAction can call info and error on the adapter transparently.
Key Takeaway

Adapters should be small translation layers that delegate to the adaptee; avoid embedding business logic in the adapter itself.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity

PayPalAdapter starter code

<!-- Starter code from the chapter; implement PayPalAdapter -->
// Adaptee: Legacy PayPal Gateway
class PayPalGateway {
  public void makePayment(double amount, String currency) {
    System.out.println("Processing payment of " + currency + " " + amount + " via PayPal (Legacy).");
  }
}

// Target: New Payment Processor interface
interface PaymentProcessor {
  void processPayment(double amount); // Assumes USD
}

// TODO: Implement the PayPalAdapter here
class PayPalAdapter implements PaymentProcessor {
  private PayPalGateway payPalGateway;

  public PayPalAdapter(PayPalGateway payPalGateway) {
    this.payPalGateway = payPalGateway;
  }

  @Override
  public void processPayment(double amount) {
    // Adapt the new interface call to the old one, assuming USD
    payPalGateway.makePayment(amount, "USD");
  }
}
What to test:
  • Create a PayPalGateway, wrap it with PayPalAdapter, and call processPayment from an ECommerceApp client.
  • Confirm the legacy makePayment output shows the USD amount and message.
  • Ensure adapter does not modify PayPalGateway; the adapter only translates calls.
Key Takeaway

An object adapter centralizes interface translation and protects legacy code from change while enabling new clients to use it.

screens.title: What is the Decorator pattern?
screens.narratorSegment: Decorator is a structural pattern that lets you attach additional responsibilities to an object at runtime by wrapping it in decorator objects that implement the same interface. Instead of creating a rigid inheritance tree with many subclasses for every combination of features, decorators compose behavior: each decorator wraps a component and adds a single responsibility while delegating the original calls. A concrete example from the chapter is a SimpleCoffee component implementing Coffee with getDescription and getCost. Concrete decorators like MilkDecorator and SugarDecorator extend an abstract CoffeeDecorator, hold a reference to a Coffee, and add to the description and cost. You can wrap a SimpleCoffee first with MilkDecorator and then with SugarDecorator to get combined features. A common error is designing a decorator that doesn't share the component's interface; the decorator must be interchangeable with the original component so clients can use wrapped objects transparently. Decorators encourage single-responsibility and composition, making it easy to add, remove, or reorder features at runtime without modifying the base class. What is the Decorator pattern? means decorator wraps and delegates to a component while adding behavior, enabling flexible composition of responsibilities.. In practical terms, attach responsibilities to objects dynamically by wrapping them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Decorator wraps and delegates to a component while adding behavior, enabling flexible composition of responsibilities.

content.html:
Core Concept

Decorator — attach responsibilities

Decorators implement the same interface as the component and wrap an instance to add behavior while delegating the base calls.

Why use decorators
They let you mix and match features at runtime without creating many subclasses.
Correct structure
Decorator must implement the component's interface and hold a reference to a component to delegate core behavior.
Key Takeaway

Use Decorator to add features in configurable combinations while keeping the base component unchanged.

Analogy
Coffee topping analogy
Start with a simple coffee. Add milk, then sugar, then caramel as independent wrappers. Each topping modifies description and cost without changing the base coffee.
Real-world example
Java I/O streams are decorators: you can wrap a FileInputStream in a BufferedInputStream and then in a DataInputStream to add buffering and primitive reading.

screens.title: Coffee Decorator example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's examine the Coffee example from the chapter. The component interface Coffee defines getDescription and getCost. SimpleCoffee implements those methods as the base object. CoffeeDecorator is an abstract class implementing Coffee and holding a reference to another Coffee instance. Concrete decorators such as MilkDecorator and SugarDecorator extend CoffeeDecorator and override getDescription and getCost to add their own contribution and delegate to the wrapped component. This structure lets you start with a SimpleCoffee and wrap it multiple times, creating combinations like SimpleCoffee → MilkDecorator → SugarDecorator; calls to getCost traverse the wrapper chain, each decorator adding its own increment. A practical point: decorators should focus on a single responsibility and preserve the component interface so nested wrapping remains transparent to clients. Misconceptions include storing state incorrectly in decorators or making decorators not interchangeable with components. Keep each decorator stateless or confined to its behavior and ensure it delegates unchanged responsibilities to the wrapped component. In practical terms, see how decorators add description and cost to a base component. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Coffee, Decorator, and Concrete Decorators

<!-- Coffee decorator example from the chapter; angle brackets escaped -->
// Component
interface Coffee {
  String getDescription();
  double getCost();
}

// Concrete Component
class SimpleCoffee implements Coffee {
  @Override
  public String getDescription() { return "Simple Coffee"; }
  @Override
  public double getCost() { return 2.0; }
}

// Decorator
abstract class CoffeeDecorator implements Coffee {
  protected Coffee decoratedCoffee;
  public CoffeeDecorator(Coffee decoratedCoffee) { this.decoratedCoffee = decoratedCoffee; }
  @Override
  public String getDescription() { return decoratedCoffee.getDescription(); }
  @Override
  public double getCost() { return decoratedCoffee.getCost(); }
}

// MilkDecorator
class MilkDecorator extends CoffeeDecorator {
  public MilkDecorator(Coffee decoratedCoffee) { super(decoratedCoffee); }
  @Override
  public String getDescription() { return decoratedCoffee.getDescription() + ", Milk"; }
  @Override
  public double getCost() { return decoratedCoffee.getCost() + 0.5; }
}
Explanation
Wrapping order matters
Each decorator delegates to its wrapped component, so the final description and cost reflect the entire chain.
Composability
You can create any combination of features, for example new CaramelDecorator(new MilkDecorator(new SimpleCoffee())).
Testing tip
Test decorators individually by wrapping a simple component and verifying description and cost increments.
Key Takeaway

Decorators compose behavior by wrapping components; keep decorators focused and ensure they implement the same interface as the component.

screens.title: Adapter vs Decorator
screens.narratorSegment: Adapter and Decorator are both structural patterns, but they solve different problems. Adapter changes an object's interface so a client can use it; its goal is compatibility. Decorator preserves the component interface while adding behavior; its goal is flexible extension. Structurally, an adapter implements the target interface and delegates to an adaptee, often translating method names or parameter formats. A decorator implements the same interface as the component and wraps that component, adding behavior before or after delegating calls. Use Adapter when integrating legacy systems or third-party libraries without modifying them. Use Decorator when you want to add or combine responsibilities at runtime without proliferating subclasses. A common confusion arises when a wrapper both translates interface and adds behavior; decide whether the primary purpose is compatibility (Adapter) or extension (Decorator). When in doubt, keep responsibility single-purpose: an adapter should focus on translation; a decorator should focus on augmenting behavior. Adapter vs Decorator means adapter = interface translation for compatibility. decorator = behavior composition for flexible extension.. In practical terms, compare purpose, structure, and common use-cases. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison

Adapter vs Decorator

Adapter (Compatibility)
  • Purpose: Convert interface to match client expectations.
  • Structure: Implements target, delegates to adaptee.
  • Use-case: Integrate legacy or third-party code.
Decorator (Extension)
  • Purpose: Add responsibilities dynamically to an object.
  • Structure: Implements component interface, wraps a component instance.
  • Use-case: Compose features like toppings or stream wrappers.
Quick rule

If you need compatibility, adapt. If you need extensibility and composability, decorate.

screens.title: Design considerations & best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Design discipline matters when implementing these patterns. For adapters, keep the translation code minimal: map parameters, convert formats, and delegate to the adaptee. Avoid embedding validation or business rules across your system inside adapters. Prefer dependency injection so adapters can be tested with mocks. For decorators, aim for single-responsibility: each decorator should add one concern, like buffering, spell checking, or adding sugar to coffee. Ensure decorators share the component interface so they remain interchangeable. Watch out for ordering: the sequence of decorators may affect results, so document and test common compositions. Also avoid storing mutable shared state across decorators unless you design explicit coordination. Finally, use these patterns to reduce coupling: both Adapter and Decorator can help make code more modular and easier to change, but misuse — such as fat adapters that do too much or decorators that leak internal state — undermines clarity. Keep classes small, well-documented, and covered with unit tests exercising adapters and decorator chains. Design considerations & best practices means use dependency injection for adapters, single-responsibility for decorators, and unit tests for composition order and behavior.. In practical terms, keep adapters thin and decorators focused. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Design Guidance

Practical rules for implementation

Adapters: keep them thin
Map signatures, convert formats, and delegate. Inject the adaptee to enable testing.
Decorators: single responsibility
Each decorator should add one concern and be interchangeable with the component.
Testing & order
Write unit tests for adapters and decorator chains, and verify ordering effects explicitly.
Key Takeaway

Apply small, focused adapters and decorators. Use DI, single responsibility, and tests to keep compositions reliable and maintainable.

Example caution
Avoid decorators that change the component contract; they must remain interchangeable.

screens.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
screens.narratorSegment: This screen covers common pitfalls that learners often run into. First, confusing Adapter with Facade: Adapter converts one interface to another for compatibility with a specific client, while Facade offers a simplified interface to an entire subsystem for many clients. If your goal is to reduce complexity across the system, consider a Facade; if your goal is to reuse a specific existing class with a different client interface, use Adapter. Second, in decorator implementations ensure the decorator and component share the same interface; failing to do so means clients can't use wrapped objects interchangeably, defeating the purpose of decoration. Third, avoid placing business logic or stateful coordination inside adapters — they should be focused translators. Fourth, avoid decorators that hold mutable shared state across layers unless explicitly designed, because ordering will then produce subtle bugs. Finally, watch dependency ownership: adapters should not assume ownership of adaptees (don't close or dispose resources unexpectedly). These mistakes can make systems brittle; careful adherence to pattern structure avoids them. Common mistakes and misconceptions means don't conflate adapter with facade; keep adapters thin and decorators interface-compatible and stateless when possible.. Common Mistakes

Avoid these traps

Adapter vs Facade
Adapter remaps an interface for compatibility with a client; Facade simplifies a whole subsystem for many clients.
Decorator interface mismatch
If a decorator does not implement the component interface, it cannot be substituted for the component and breaks transparency.
Fat adapters
Adapters that embed heavy business logic create hidden responsibilities and increase coupling; keep them focused.
Stateful decorators
Avoid shared mutable state unless explicitly required and well-documented; ordering and interleaving can otherwise break behavior.
Quick warning

Follow the pattern contracts: interfaces for decorators and minimal translation for adapters — this prevents fragile designs.

content.html:
Activity Guidance

Text Editor Decorators

<!-- Starter code; implement the concrete decorators as below -->
// Component
interface Editor { void write(String text); }

// Concrete Component
class BasicTextEditor implements Editor {
  @Override
  public void write(String text) {
    System.out.println("Basic Editor writes: '" + text + "'");
  }
}

// Decorator Abstract Class
abstract class EditorDecorator implements Editor {
  protected Editor decoratedEditor;
  public EditorDecorator(Editor decoratedEditor) { this.decoratedEditor = decoratedEditor; }
  @Override
  public void write(String text) { decoratedEditor.write(text); }
}

// SpellCheckDecorator and AutoSaveDecorator -- implement these
Implementation notes:
  • SpellCheckDecorator should inspect the text, print a message about corrections, then delegate write.
  • AutoSaveDecorator should delegate write first, then print an auto-save confirmation.
  • Compose decorators to verify order and behavior in the console output.
Key Takeaway

Decorators allow you to mix features like spell check and auto-save without changing the editor implementation or creating many subclasses.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on two structural patterns that shape how objects relate and evolve in a system. First, Adapter solves the problem of incompatible interfaces: it translates one interface into another so existing classes can be used by new clients without changing either side. Think of a travel plug adapter that translates an unfamiliar plug shape so the device still gets power. Second, Decorator offers a way to add responsibilities to objects at runtime by wrapping them, avoiding subclass explosion when you need many feature combinations. You will encounter concrete Java examples: an OldLogger adapted to a NewLogger interface, and Coffee objects wrapped with Milk, Sugar, and Caramel decorators so costs and descriptions change dynamically. We will also compare object adapter versus class adapter, highlight common mistakes, and walk through hands-on starter tasks adapting a legacy payment gateway and decorating a basic editor. By the end of this chapter you’ll know when to translate an interface versus when to layer behavior, and you’ll be able to implement and combine these patterns in realistic Java code. Start by exploring the three topics shown below to build intuition before we dive into code and exercises.

These objectives map to practical skills you will use when designing maintainable systems. First, you will implement the Adapter pattern to convert an existing class interface into the interface your client expects. This includes writing an adapter that delegates calls to an adaptee instance. Second, you will distinguish class adapters (inheritance-based) from object adapters (composition-based), and understand why object adapters are usually preferred in Java. Third, you will identify scenarios where Adapter is the right choice, such as integrating legacy code or third-party libraries without modifying them. Each objective shows a clear skill and why it matters: adapters preserve working code and avoid risky rewrites. You will also implement the Decorator pattern to attach responsibilities to an object dynamically, and understand how this pattern offers a more flexible alternative to subclassing. Finally, you will apply decorators to real objects so behavior can be composed at runtime. Together these objectives prepare you to choose whether to translate an interface or to wrap behavior, and to implement both patterns safely in Java.

This page extends the objectives with applied scenarios you will practice. You will be able to identify when Adapter is the correct pattern: when a client expects a specific interface and an existing class provides needed behavior but uses different method names or argument formats. A concrete measurable outcome is writing an adapter that makes a legacy PayPal gateway usable by your new payment-processing interface. You will also recognize when Decorator is a better fit: when additional responsibilities must be combined in flexible ways, such as adding spell check and auto-save to a text editor without creating separate subclasses for every combination. Your outcome will be implementing concrete decorators like SpellCheckDecorator and AutoSaveDecorator and composing them to add both behaviors. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or diagram to help recall: think 'plug' for Adapter and 'layers' for Decorator. Finally, you will be able to explain common mistakes, such as confusing Adapter with Facade or implementing a decorator that does not match the component interface. These skills make your designs resilient and easier to extend over time.

Adapter is a structural pattern whose purpose is to make two incompatible interfaces work together. The pattern introduces an adapter class that implements the interface expected by the client and internally delegates calls to the adaptee, the existing class with a different A P I. A concrete example is adapting a legacy logger with a single logMessage method so it can be used where a client expects separate info and error methods. This avoids modifying stable legacy code or rewriting the client. Remember there are two implementation strategies: class adapter, which uses inheritance, and object adapter, which uses composition. In Java, object adapters are far more common because Java does not support multiple class inheritance; composition is safer and more flexible. A common misconception is to confuse Adapter with Facade. Adapter converts one interface to another for a specific client need, while Facade provides a simplified interface over a subsystem for many clients. When you need to adapt an old A P I to a new interface for a particular use, Adapter is the right fit. Consider whether you need to translate method signatures or to hide complexity; that distinction will guide your pattern choice.

There are two conceptual implementation strategies for Adapter: class adapters and object adapters. Class adapters use inheritance: the adapter inherits from the adaptee and from the target interface type, effectively becoming both. This approach can work when adapting interfaces or in languages with multiple inheritance, but in Java it's rarely used because Java does not permit inheriting from two concrete classes. Object adapters use composition: the adapter implements the target interface and holds a reference to an adaptee instance. Calls on the adapter translate into calls on the adaptee. This composition approach is more flexible: you can adapt different concrete adaptees without changing the adapter class, and you avoid the brittle coupling inheritance creates. A simple process to implement an object adapter is: define the target interface, hold an adaptee instance inside the adapter, implement target methods by delegating or translating calls to the adaptee, and construct the adapter with a specific adaptee. A common mistake is attempting to force a class adapter design in Java; prefer composition and keep adapters small and focused on translating behavior, not re-implementing it.

Let's walk through a concrete object adapter example that appears in the chapter source. We have an existing OldLogger class with a single method that logs messages in a legacy format. The new client expects a NewLogger interface with info and error methods. The adapter implements NewLogger and holds an OldLogger instance. When the client calls info on the adapter, the adapter translates that into a logMessage call on the OldLogger, typically adding a prefix like INFO. The same goes for error. This translation preserves the legacy implementation while matching the client's expectations. When reading the code, pay attention to delegation and to how the adapter's constructor receives the adaptee instance — that dependency injection keeps the adapter testable and decoupled from concrete adaptee construction. A misconception is to implement heavy logic inside the adapter; instead, keep translations small and clear. After you read the code panel, imagine substituting a different logging adaptee: the adapter remains the same because it depends on the adaptee interface or concrete instance handed to it. Object Adapter: OldLoggerAdapter example means keep adapter logic minimal: translate signatures and delegate behavior. inject the adaptee so the adapter remains testable.. In practical terms, walk through the adapter that makes oldlogger fulfill newlogger. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This activity asks you to implement an object adapter for a legacy PayPal gateway. The legacy class provides makePayment(amount, currency). Your new system expects a PaymentProcessor with processPayment(amount) that assumes USD. The correct approach is to implement a PayPalAdapter that implements PaymentProcessor, holds a PayPalGateway instance, and translates processPayment into makePayment using USD. The adapter should be constructed with the existing gateway so you don't alter legacy code. This pattern supports using the same adapter in multiple clients and keeps the translation logic in one place. When you implement this, ensure you only change the adapter code, not the legacy gateway or the client. A misconception to avoid is adding currency logic broadly across the app; adapter centralizes translation. After implementing, test with an ECommerceApp client that calls checkout and confirms that makePayment prints the expected message. This mirrors the example in the source and demonstrates a real integration scenario you'll face in the field. Activity: PayPalGateway → PaymentProcessor (Object Adapter) means write a paypaladapter that implements paymentprocessor and delegates to paypalgateway.makepayment using usd.. In practical terms, implement paypaladapter to adapt legacy gateway to a new interface. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Decorator is a structural pattern that lets you attach additional responsibilities to an object at runtime by wrapping it in decorator objects that implement the same interface. Instead of creating a rigid inheritance tree with many subclasses for every combination of features, decorators compose behavior: each decorator wraps a component and adds a single responsibility while delegating the original calls. A concrete example from the chapter is a SimpleCoffee component implementing Coffee with getDescription and getCost. Concrete decorators like MilkDecorator and SugarDecorator extend an abstract CoffeeDecorator, hold a reference to a Coffee, and add to the description and cost. You can wrap a SimpleCoffee first with MilkDecorator and then with SugarDecorator to get combined features. A common error is designing a decorator that doesn't share the component's interface; the decorator must be interchangeable with the original component so clients can use wrapped objects transparently. Decorators encourage single-responsibility and composition, making it easy to add, remove, or reorder features at runtime without modifying the base class. Adapter and Decorator are both structural patterns, but they solve different problems. Adapter changes an object's interface so a client can use it; its goal is compatibility. Decorator preserves the component interface while adding behavior; its goal is flexible extension. Structurally, an adapter implements the target interface and delegates to an adaptee, often translating method names or parameter formats. A decorator implements the same interface as the component and wraps that component, adding behavior before or after delegating calls. Use Adapter when integrating legacy systems or third-party libraries without modifying them. Use Decorator when you want to add or combine responsibilities at runtime without proliferating subclasses. A common confusion arises when a wrapper both translates interface and adds behavior; decide whether the primary purpose is compatibility (Adapter) or extension (Decorator). When in doubt, keep responsibility single-purpose: an adapter should focus on translation; a decorator should focus on augmenting behavior. Design discipline matters when implementing these patterns. For adapters, keep the translation code minimal: map parameters, convert formats, and delegate to the adaptee. Avoid embedding validation or business rules across your system inside adapters. Prefer dependency injection so adapters can be tested with mocks. For decorators, aim for single-responsibility: each decorator should add one concern, like buffering, spell checking, or adding sugar to coffee. Ensure decorators share the component interface so they remain interchangeable. Watch out for ordering: the sequence of decorators may affect results, so document and test common compositions. Also avoid storing mutable shared state across decorators unless you design explicit coordination. Finally, use these patterns to reduce coupling: both Adapter and Decorator can help make code more modular and easier to change, but misuse — such as fat adapters that do too much or decorators that leak internal state — undermines clarity. Keep classes small, well-documented, and covered with unit tests exercising adapters and decorator chains. This screen covers common pitfalls that learners often run into. First, confusing Adapter with Facade: Adapter converts one interface to another for compatibility with a specific client, while Facade offers a simplified interface to an entire subsystem for many clients. If your goal is to reduce complexity across the system, consider a Facade; if your goal is to reuse a specific existing class with a different client interface, use Adapter. Second, in decorator implementations ensure the decorator and component share the same interface; failing to do so means clients can't use wrapped objects interchangeably, defeating the purpose of decoration. Third, avoid placing business logic or stateful coordination inside adapters — they should be focused translators. Fourth, avoid decorators that hold mutable shared state across layers unless explicitly designed, because ordering will then produce subtle bugs. Finally, watch dependency ownership: adapters should not assume ownership of adaptees (don't close or dispose resources unexpectedly). These mistakes can make systems brittle; careful adherence to pattern structure avoids them. These three key concepts summarize the chapter. First, Adapter: it converts the interface of an existing class into the interface clients expect so incompatible pieces can work together. Think Target, Adaptee, Adapter as the trio of roles. Second, Object Adapter vs Class Adapter: prefer object adapters in Java because composition is flexible and avoids multiple inheritance issues. Third, Decorator: wrap a component with decorator objects that implement the same interface to attach responsibilities dynamically, avoiding subclass combinatorial explosion. Keep decorators focused and ensure they remain interchangeable with the component. Remember practical examples: adapting an OldLogger to a NewLogger, adapting a legacy payment gateway with PayPalAdapter, and decorating SimpleCoffee with Milk and Sugar to change description and cost. These core ideas will guide design choices when integrating legacy code or composing features dynamically.

Before you start implementing, keep three short reminders in mind. First, identify the problem: interface mismatch suggests Adapter; need for combinable features suggests Decorator. Second, prefer object adapters and dependency injection in Java so adapters stay decoupled and testable. Third, design decorators with single responsibilities and ensure they implement the component interface so they remain interchangeable. Practically, when you see legacy code that works but has the wrong method names, write a small adapter. When you need many feature combinations, wrap the base object in decorators. These principles help you modify and extend systems safely without rewriting stable code or creating brittle class hierarchies. When you code, write unit tests that confirm translation behavior for adapters and composition order for decorators — tests reveal ordering issues and hidden state in wrapped chains.
